  78. The disagreement here concerns demonstration, not merely a contest of opinions. The illuminationist philosopher argues according to his own principles, while the author argues both from his principles and from those of the philosophers in Aristotle’s school. One example is the author's acceptance of substantial forms joined to matter and responsible for things' distinctive effects. The philosopher of illumination, by contrast, speaks of forms separate from matter that act upon it: the governing beings he calls the lords of species.

    The author is right that the unity of God, both in Himself and in His action, does not require us to deny created powers. Powers joined to physical things are instruments through which God acts. The higher beings that are separate from matter are also His instruments, or, in another image, eyes through which His governance is displayed. Scripture itself speaks of God's hosts and describes Him as exalted in rank and Lord of the Throne.

    On the illuminationist account, the single reality does not differ in level, still less in number or kind. Its differences arise from the ways it appears to receivers with different capacities.

    An objection arises: the philosopher of illumination also speaks of powers. What can he mean by them if, throughout the body, only the soul acts? Consider the imagination. For the author, it is the soul appearing as a particular active power, able to perceive images free from matter though not from size. The power that forms bodily shapes, or the power by which a plant grows, is likewise the soul operating in a particular way without leaving its higher level. In the illuminationist account, imagination can instead be understood as the soul or intellect appearing through a receptive power joined to a bodily condition. The same can be said of the other powers. In this sense it is reasonable to say that the illuminationist philosopher did not abolish powers altogether.

  82. A preparatory cause is something whose presence, and then its passing away, helps make another thing possible. We must distinguish three cases. A positive cause is something on whose presence the result depends. An obstacle is something whose absence is required. A preparatory condition is involved in bringing about the state from which the result can occur. I take the philosopher's remark to be directed at people who multiply the soul's powers and then call them mere preparations for the giver of forms. Their position rejects the view, held by some theologians, that one created act generates the next—for example, that moving a hand directly generates the movement of a key, or that premises generate a conclusion.

    Philosophers instead distinguish the actual giver of existence from the causes that prepare things to receive it. But the word ‘preparatory’ is also used in an everyday, wider sense: a means through which the real source sends its effect. Sadra uses it this way for bodily and immaterial causes, both here and in his book on origin and return. The real giver of existence, he explains, must be free of every unfulfilled possibility, and only God is so free. All other causes are means through which His giving reaches things. A philosopher of this rank certainly knew the difference between a cause in the strict sense and a preparatory condition.

  83. In the Philosophy of Illumination, Suhrawardi offers a related explanation. Light, he says, gives of itself and has, in its very being, love for what is of its own kind and mastery over what is below it.

    When the light that governs a living body exercises mastery through that body, the power of anger arises. Through its love, the power of desire arises. The governing light also sees particular images and understands a general form that can apply to them: someone sees Zayd and Amr, for example, and grasps the human nature they share. A corresponding power of nourishment appears in the body.

    Likewise, because a complete light can be the source of another light, a power of reproduction appears in its body, bringing about another body with its own governing light. Because light can also increase through the lights that reach it and move from possibility to fulfillment, a power of growth appears in the body, enlarging it in fitting proportions.

    These bodily powers are therefore branches of the governing light. The body is its image or representation. This is a shortened account of Suhrawardi's explanation.

  101. The power also called practical reason is a power of understanding. But it deals specifically with particular matters connected with what we do, such as how to use our powers of perception and movement. The other power, theoretical reason, deals with what can be understood apart from such particular actions. This distinction underlies the difference between practical and theoretical wisdom.

    Particular actions here include more than everyday work. They include actions directed toward the life to come, such as justice and kindness done for worthy and firmly established ends. They also include the work of ordinary living, such as building a house so carefully that it serves the purposes for which it was made.

  102. The power of desire serves practical reason in a human being, just as it serves the powers of judgment and imagination in an animal. When desire serves practical reason, we call it will. When it serves the animal power of judgment, we call it appetite.

    Consider visiting someone who is ill. If a person does this for God's sake, the action belongs to practical and theoretical reason. If the aim is to gain a pleasure or benefit imagined by the mind or felt by the senses, it belongs to the animal powers of perception and movement.

  103. Suppose we begin with the general rule, “Every good action ought to be done.” Add the statement, “Telling the truth is good.” Together these give us the general conclusion, “Telling the truth ought to be done.” Theoretical reason understands that general judgment.

    When practical reason faces a particular choice, it says, “This act would be truthful. Every truthful act ought to be done. So this act ought to be done.” The judgment now concerns something we can actually do. Practical reason has reached it with help from theoretical reason.

    These are two levels of one intellect, not two wholly separate powers. Theoretical reason understands things we cannot bring about by our own actions. Practical reason understands how we are to act.

    ↩

  104. Practical reason usually begins from common beliefs and experience, though some of its starting points can be self-evident or well tested.

    ↩

  105. The commentator says that careful attention to Avicenna's account shows that there is one judge within us, not several separate selves.

    ↩

  106. The soul remains the underlying source of its powers, and those powers are different levels at which it appears. Each level, considered only in its own particular form, is not the whole soul. As explained earlier, the soul has both multiplicity within unity and unity within multiplicity.

    The author points out that to know the soul properly we should first understand existence itself and its different levels. The strongest explanation is one that moves from cause to effect. This is one way to understand the saying, “Whoever knows himself knows his Lord.” We come to know the laws and qualities of the Lord first, and then, by their light, know the soul. Knowledge of the former becomes the measure of knowledge of the latter. Other interpretations of the saying were discussed earlier.

    ↩

  107. The intellect's early need for the body's powers is part of its development. It does not mean that the intellect always depends on them.

    ↩

  108. Strength and nobility are different qualities. A soul may have strength without nobility, nobility without strength, or both.

  109. A person may smell one thing, hear another, and write something else at the same time. They do not confuse these activities, and they can tell their different qualities apart. The common sense that brings perceptions together offers an example, however small, of a being whom no activity distracts from another.

    This is especially clear on the author's account, which holds that the soul actively produces its perceptions of particular things. When something visible is before it, a sound is heard, a smell reaches it, food is tasted, and something is touched, the soul can grasp all these things at once.

    The same applies, at a higher level, to the simple intellect that gives rise to detailed acts of understanding. This is the settled ability to know. It grasps many things in one enduring act, even when no separate images of those things pass through the imagination in sequence. Ask someone who possesses this ability a number of different questions: they can see the answers together before putting them into words one by one.

    Someone might think that the answers were not known until they were separately expressed, and that the knowledge was merely close at hand beforehand, unlike the distant possibility of knowledge in an uneducated person. But that confuses a lack of separate images in the imagination with a lack of intellectual knowledge. It also confuses the absence of many separate forms with the presence of one complete and powerful form of understanding. This unified light makes the different objects of knowledge clear to the intellect itself, even before they become clear to its imagination, its senses, or anyone else.

    A human being is more than imagination and sensation. The intellect is the highest level of the person, and the other powers draw on it. Nor is this knowledge merely vague. Existence is light; the stronger and more unified that light is, the better it can reveal differences within what it knows. Many things can be known more distinctly through one comprehensive act of understanding than through scattered acts. In the same way, all fixed realities are eternally known to God in perfect detail.

    ↩

  110. “The first” and “the second” refer to strength or weakness in the soul's sensory and intellectual levels.

    ↩

  111. Learned virtues are valuable too. The commentator notes that Aristotle calls freedom a “settled quality,” which can suggest a virtue developed through repeated practice.

    ↩

  112. The two virtues are wisdom and freedom. Together they mean readiness to understand many things and to become less attached to matter.

    ↩

  113. Justice is the balance among the soul's four main powers. The power of knowledge means readiness of the theoretical intellect.

    ↩

  114. Too much practical thought becomes cleverness used to gain worldly benefits and avoid harm. Too little neglects practical judgment. The virtue lies between these extremes.

    ↩

  115. Knowledge of the truth is the source of many goods, but it also bears a relation to the wisdom of character. Near the end of the Metaphysics of the Healing, Avicenna limits wisdom as a character trait to balanced thinking about everyday affairs. It would be better not to limit it in that way, since our thinking also concerns matters of theory.

    This does not mean that examining difficult questions too deeply is a vice. The search for truth is good. The fault lies in shifting endlessly among opinions without reaching sound conclusions because one has neglected the sustained study of real knowledge. Such a person may still discuss difficult ideas with great confidence. The appearance of learning is then like the swelling of a sick body mistaken for healthy strength, or like smoke without fire. Spending time with such people can spread this habit, just as certain company can encourage ignorance or foolishness.

    We must distinguish wisdom as knowledge from wisdom as a trait of character. The first is knowing things as they truly are. We should seek more of it, as in the prayer, “My Lord, increase me in knowledge.” The second concerns sound judgment and moderation in conduct. It is one part of justice and calls for balance.

    Some people confuse this character trait with practical philosophy, the branch of learning distinguished from theoretical philosophy. But practical philosophy is also knowledge, and more of it is desirable. It concerns what lies within our choice: how communities are governed, how households are managed, and how character is improved. This is knowledge about conduct. Wisdom as part of justice is the character trait itself, not a field of study.

    Moderation, courage, generosity, and wisdom can each be natural or acquired. Some people are born inclined toward them; others naturally incline in the opposite direction. As Ali said: “I have seen reason in two forms, inborn and learned; learned reason cannot help where inborn reason is absent.” We are not commanded to produce gifts of nature. We are responsible for the virtues we can acquire, so that the soul becomes “light upon light.” Practising good habits, avoiding both excess and deficiency, keeping good company, and avoiding corrupt company strengthen natural virtues. Where a natural tendency is weak, practice can bring it nearer to completion.

This concerns substances. For quantities, think of one continuous line, such as the axis of that sphere, or of a line imagined as infinite. Think also of time as one continuous movement from God and towards God. We divide a line by imagined points and time by imagined instants, days, hours, minutes, seconds, and so on. The divisions do not make the underlying continuity a multitude of separate things.

  133. Up to this point, the person is usually only a natural human being. The useful test is whether the powers of imagination have become established.     In a similar way, a person remains at the level of the soul until the power to grasp things through thought develops. The person then becomes a human being at the level of intellect. This is especially true when sensed things and imagined pictures become mirrors through which the mind grasps what it can understand without them. The person has then passed beyond shifting states and reached a steadier condition. As the Qur'an says, “Remain upright, as you have been commanded.”

  134. If we define a human being through the parts of a definition, the complete definition is a rational animal. “Animal” alone is not enough, and neither is “rational” alone. Likewise, if we describe the parts that exist in the world, a complete human being consists of soul and body.

    The human being considered at the spiritual level is the soul; the natural human being is the body. But the full human being is the union of the two. It might be better to remove the word “here,” since the author's purpose is to show that becoming free from matter does not mean simply throwing the body away. It means the body's existence becomes subtler and more complete. Perhaps, however, “here” is meant to describe the two as united.

    In any event, this discussion challenges those who suppose that a human being is nothing but the soul.

  135. The body grows more subtle and unified as the soul develops. The commentator says this finer body is the imaginal body.

  136. The soul's direct, essential care is for the imaginal body, not the dead material body. The latter is only a shell.

  137. The afterlife body is related to the soul as light is to its source, though the perfected intellect may no longer attend to its body.

  138. More precisely, what the perceiver grasps becomes free from matter along with the perceiver, because the two are united in the act of understanding. At both levels, the earth is changed into another earth: dark, material existence gives way to a brighter existence in the form of an image, more complete and more lasting.

    Since what makes a thing what it is lies in its form, the perfection reached at the higher level completes the lower one. Indeed, that higher perfection is the lower one's own perfection. All forms rise until they no longer depend on matter and join the pure forms of the world of images. This means that their separate character is absorbed and disappears there. Souls likewise grow more complete until they join the intellects. Even animal souls join the higher realities governing their kinds and share in their gathering after death, though only as followers.

  139. An ascent from one level to a higher one is a change that makes a thing more complete. In this kind of ascent, the earlier level is not taken off and replaced, as happens in a change from one opposed state to another. What falls away is only its deficiency and limitation. The later level retains the perfection of the earlier one and adds something to it. It is a putting-on followed by another putting-on, rather than a taking-off followed by a putting-on.

    Every power present in the natural human being is present more fully in the human being at the level of the soul, and more fully still in the human being at the level of intellect. As discussed earlier, at the highest level those powers are gathered into one, because it belongs to the realm in which things are united. In this sense, God's hand is with the gathered community.

  140. The natural human being senses things through bodily organs. The human being at the level of intellect, being more complete and self-sufficient, knows directly through the self. At that level, immediate awareness serves the role of hearing and sight.

    A natural person who attends to one sensation is drawn away from another. At the intellectual level, one act of awareness does not prevent another: a thing is known together with other things. This is one reason for saying that such a person grasps more things, including universal realities. Some earlier philosophers likewise say that God knows a particular thing “in a universal way.” Their point is that He knows the particular together with every other particular, in one timeless act.

    Since intellectual knowledge is direct presence, its vision reaches higher realities free from matter. Through one act of seeing it grasps what belongs to the world of intellect, and what can be seen in the worlds of image and nature. What a lower power sees is included in that higher seeing. The same principle applies to the other senses.

  141. The claim applies to souls generally, including the souls of animals and celestial beings.

  142. The commentator thinks a few words may be missing from the source passage.

  143. Here, “image” means a likeness or representation, not an object of worship.

  144. This seeing takes place through the intellect as it rises toward completion, in the bright side of the heart. There the person does not hear the distancing answer, “You shall not see Me.” The Lord of lords speaks otherwise. A person should therefore become good through the full development of practical reason, which guides action, and excellent through the full development of the intellect that knows. More than that, the mountain of the separate self must be broken down, as the mountain of independent existence is broken down in the earlier image. Only then does the person become fully human in actuality.

    The first human being in the world of intellect is a brilliant, piercing light containing every human state—that is, every human perfection. There is nothing astonishing, for God, in gathering a whole world into one being. Yet those perfections exist there in a higher way. This is an example of a figure of speech that appears to qualify praise but actually increases it, as in the saying, “I am the most eloquent of people—though I come from Quraysh.”

    This is the human being whom Plato described when speaking of the divine forms. He distinguished two meanings of human: the visible, perishable human being and an enduring human reality that neither decays nor disappears and that cares for its kind. Plato, however, added something to the definition: he said that this enduring human being uses the body. (In manuscripts of the book on the soul that we have seen, the wording “because he added to its definition” is an error.)

    The definition should have stopped at the shining light containing all human perfections in full actuality. The use of the body and its powers involves need and limitation, whereas an intellect fully developed involves perfection and freedom from need. Plato must therefore have meant that the body is used in a secondary way, through the soul, to bring other things to completion—not because the higher human reality needs the body in order to complete itself.

    The rational soul's use of the body, through the truth and for the truth, follows from its connection with that higher reality. It is as though the soul has already taken off the cloak it still appears to wear. This is the point of the statement that follows: when the animal soul becomes a soul of the lower spiritual world, working with imagined and mathematically conceived forms to grasp general truths, the rational soul in full activity comes into being at a higher level. It then gives that lower spiritual soul a nobler life, belonging to the world of intellect. We have already seen that the earlier mode of being of the universal intellect can also be attributed to the soul; this is the basis for speaking of the soul as ancient in time. The same applies to the intellect's later mode of being. This makes the matter clearer. — S. R.

  158. The author means definitions and descriptions. It is not enough to memorize a definition of the Active Intellect—for example, that it needs no matter either to exist or to act, that it has no unrealized capacity waiting to be fulfilled, and that it stands as a universal source in relation to the individual intellects that are already thinking. A person may know all these features so well that the knowledge has become a settled habit, yet still fall short.

    The soul must itself become independent of the body and its powers, let go of narrow personal aims, rise above ends invented by imagination, and grow fuller in its own existence. It must join that higher intellect and endure through its endurance—or, more truly, through God's endurance. The universal intellect is God's word, power, and will. In short, take on the qualities of spiritual beings, and, in the proper sense, the qualities of God.

  159. Perhaps Avicenna was simply not in a state to give an answer when the question was put to him. A person is not always in the same condition. As the Persian verse says:

    At times I sit upon the highest roof; At times I cannot see the ground beneath my feet.

    The fact that different things receive a power in different ways is one matter. But the author is right that the soul's unity is not the unity of a single item counted alongside others. It is a unity that gathers many powers into itself. We could call it a true unity reflected at a lower level.

    Earlier discussions showed that all eight kinds of acting can be found in the soul. Spiritual teachers also speak of seven subtle levels within a person, beginning with nature. In a complete human being, powers that are scattered through different levels of the world come together. When no power is missing, no corresponding act need be missing either.

  160. Plants and animals are singled out because their material parts are continually breaking down and being replaced. This is especially evident in animals. In the medical account being used here, the causes include several kinds of heat: heat linked to the elements, to the body's own constitution, to the heavens, and to bodily and inward movements. The movement of breath and blood outward or inward during anger, joy, fear, sorrow, and similar states is discussed elsewhere.

    But the difficulty disappears if we attend to the unchanging aspect of each thing that points toward God. A thing's existence is what gives it stability, unity, and its own identity. It is like a fixed place for washing beside water that never stops flowing.

    While you imagine yourself in front and behind, You are bound to the body and deprived of the soul. Above, below, before, behind belong to the body; The bright reality of the soul has no direction.

    By “instruments,” the author means the animal power of judgment and the brain. By the “shadows” among which an animal shares awareness, he means the images in its inner powers of perception. It grasps an image in common with other images without clearly distinguishing one from another, rather as a person may recognize something under a general description without seeing what makes it particular.

  176. Do not miss this point. Something that exists at the level of intellect does not have a firm place there until it has become a complete intellectual reality. It reaches that state by acquiring the distinguishing forms that complete its intellectual nature. Knowing the first, basic truths—whether simple ideas or judgments—is like charcoal becoming warm. Gaining further truths through reasoning is like the charcoal changing into fire. The undeveloped soul is like charcoal; a soul that has become intellect in full is like a fire that is nothing but fire. Charcoal does not become fire merely because it has grown hot. In the same way, a human soul does not become an actual intellect merely by possessing the first truths.

    It may have reached its highest development in imagination while remaining only close to becoming an intellect in full. It has not yet become established in the intellectual world. Consider this carefully.

  177. Avicenna thought celestial souls become complete by repeatedly knowing higher beings. Sadra adds that they also grow in their own being.

  178. This means the simple knowledge of the Necessary Being. The philosophers in Aristotle’s school call God's knowledge “intellect” or “understanding” to distinguish it from the other kinds of knowing: sensation, imagination, and the animal power of judgment.

    Avicenna did not, however, reach the deeper meaning of simple intellect. A reality wholly without parts contains all beings in a higher and more complete way. Its knowledge is direct presence and comes before the things known. Every existence is present through its own presence, and every nature is present through the divine names and qualities from which it necessarily follows.

    Avicenna's most developed claim is that the forms arise from God's own being and depend on Him as effects, not as qualities lodged within a subject. They do not come to Him as our mental representations are said to come to the soul from the Active Intellect, with the help of things perceived in the natural world. In this older account, the senses help prepare us for knowledge: one who lacks a sense lacks the knowledge normally gained through it.

  180. If God is the source of intellectual forms, He cannot lack the perfection they express.

  181. True simplicity means containing every kind of being without parts or any lack.

  182. These intellectual forms are not separate beings of that kind. They remain through God's own abiding existence, not merely because He keeps them in existence. They live through His life, not merely because He gives them life. In this sense, whoever sees them sees God. They have none of the matter, movement, or other features that mark ordinary things as separate. Even the rules that govern the distinction between one thing and another fall away at this level.

    Avicenna should have removed separation, independence, and division from these forms by understanding them as knowledge immediately present to God. If this is true of existences that still admit of some distinction, how much more is it true of intellectual forms that are free from matter? The answer cannot be to replace direct knowledge with the very separation that never existed and never will.

  183. Sadra's point is that Avicenna did not always give each matter the attention it deserved. He should, in Sadra's view, have devoted more of his time to the highest knowledge and to seeking the truth. That does not mean that mastering many branches of learning is without value. Broad knowledge is one of the highest achievements and helps students who need guidance. Sadra thinks that if Avicenna had devoted most of his attention to knowledge of God, he would have avoided some serious mistakes in philosophy. But we should be careful about the examples offered. When Avicenna does not identify one permanent reality in plants and animals, this need not mean that he has forgotten what existence itself is, or that he thinks its different levels have nothing in common.

    He does say that a cause and its effect are related in the kind of existence they have, and that existence is one reality. His Discussions and other writings bear this out. In The Divine Witnesses, Sadra himself explains that the Aristotle’s followers' apparent claim that existences differ concerns the essences described by those existences, not existence in its own right.

  185. Knowledge is one with what is known directly. Even when the object is known through a form, its essence and its existence are not wholly separated in that knowledge: what makes the knowledge of the sun different from knowledge of the moon is also what makes both instances of knowledge alike. In this sense, knowledge of the sun is knowledge shaped by the sun, and knowledge of the moon by the moon. Awareness of existence can be direct or gained through ideas. Direct awareness may be general or detailed. The first is like the holy soul's awareness of its own existence, as understood here and by Suhrawardi. The second is like the awareness of someone who has become absorbed in the reality he knows; the highest case is God's knowledge of Himself.

    Knowing existence through ideas also takes two forms. One studies its different levels by examining the essences of things, their defining features, and the qualities they may or must possess. The other knows existence through general descriptions that truly apply to it: that it overcomes nonexistence, gives things their unity and identity, is the light of reality, and is the life, love, knowledge, and awareness running through all things. Thinkers differ in how fully they understand existence by these paths. Existence is, after all, the subject of the highest philosophy.

  189. Learning about intellectual realities prepares the soul for direct awareness of them; death removes the body's distractions.

  190. Because the soul is linked with the body, people imagine themselves to occupy a low place in space and to belong to a particular date. Yet the soul in its own nature is free from spatial directions and times. On the view of philosophers who reject separate Platonic forms, even universal intellectual ideas have no location, time, or direction. How much more must this be true of the soul that forms them?

    Intellectual universals and even particular images seem weak to us partly because we treat them as mirrors in which to look at things outside us, rather than attending to the images themselves. If the soul made them its direct objects, they would grow stronger, as they do in the life to come. Those who seek universal knowledge should use particular images to reach universal meanings.

    Without these distractions, the soul could recognize that every universal has a unity that gathers many things together and a luminous presence embracing them. Its finer expressions, and the still finer expressions of those expressions, include the individual things of the worlds of image and nature. They are its lights and rays. In it there is multiplicity within unity and unity within multiplicity.

  193. The expression means “ox hunger.” The foreign term fān-būlī-mūs refers to great hunger: one part of the name means something large, like an ox, and another means hunger. In Persian, a very large thing may be likened to an ox.

    The old medical explanation is that extreme cold affects the opening of the stomach. The stomach then loses its sense of touch and no longer notices the feeling that, in that account, black bile produces to signal hunger. Its power to draw food in is also lost, to the point that the person cannot swallow a mouthful. The stomach appears satisfied, while the other organs are desperately hungry because no nourishment reaches them. The same cold is said to spread from the stomach to the organ of taste and make that sense numb. This is a description from the medical theory of the time.

  194. The point is not that imagining something strongly enough will make it appear as a real form in the next life. If that were so, everyone who enjoys comfort in this world and imagines fine food, elegant clothing, beautiful spouses, and similar pleasures would meet those very things there. Such an idea is unworthy of the author's careful teaching, as his explanations already make clear and will show again.

    Rather, good actions, the regular practice of them, the qualities of character they establish, and the fitting images through which the religious tradition describes them lead to corresponding forms in the next life. A person may be gathered with beautiful companions and pleasures suited to those actions. The same principle applies to forms of punishment. Greed, and the objects a greedy person constantly imagines, can take the form of ants with which that person is gathered. Someone who harms other Muslims, and whose thoughts are filled with ways of causing harm, may encounter that character as snakes and scorpions.

    The Qur'an says that those who wrongfully consume orphans' property are really consuming fire in their bellies. Here they consume pleasant things by unlawful means; there the same act appears as eating fire.

    Something similar happens in dreams, which resemble death in one respect. Years of plenty may appear as fat cows and years of famine as thin cows. Knowledge can appear as milk, and happiness as greenery. Each action has a meaningful, necessary connection to the form in which it appears. In the next life, people will encounter these forms as realities shaped by what they did and imagined. “People are asleep; when they die, they awaken” and discover the meanings of what they saw in this dream of earthly life. — S. R.

  229. The fire mentioned here is the fire of nature, and the water crossed is the sea of this world, sometimes called the burning sea. This concerns the Anqa. The Simurgh, ruler of the heavenly birds, is different: it represents the universal intellect, or existence flowing through all things as God's light.

    Farid al-Din Attar speaks of the Simurgh in these lines, here given in their sense:

    At the beginning, the Simurgh showed a wondrous glimpse of itself, Passing over China in the middle of the night. One feather fell there, and the whole world was stirred. Each person took an image from that feather; Whoever saw the image was filled with longing. All the works of creation shine by its splendour; Every image is an image from its feather. If the feather's image had not appeared, All this commotion would never have arisen. That feather is now in the picture-house of China: This is the meaning of “Seek knowledge, even in China.”

    The bird appearing in China stands for the universal intellect. China stands for the universal heavenly soul, at the farthest eastern reach of the spiritual world. Night is the descending order of existence, the reality expressed by the Night of Power. The fallen feather is a reflection or shadow of the intellect; the kingdoms are the turning heavens; and the image each person receives is the particular intellect.

    Attar also says that we have a king beyond Mount Qaf, named the Simurgh, king of birds: “He is close to us, and we are far from him.” Those lines point more clearly to existence flowing through all things.

  256. There are two blasts: one puts out a fire and the other lights one. Our natural bodies are like pieces of wood burning with a fire that is God's light. At the great resurrection this fire is extinguished all at once, while other pieces of wood—pure forms belonging to the next life—are lit by the souls to which they belong. Those forms become the bodies of that life.

    Look at the order of things from beginning to end. At one time the lights that govern souls are joined to material bodies; at another they are joined to the pure forms of the next life. In a limited way, this resembles our present experience: while awake, our souls are attached to natural bodies, but in sleep they appear through bodies of images. Scripture says that God takes souls at death, and also those that have not died during their sleep; He keeps those for whom death is decreed and sends the others back.

    To understand the point, consider where human beings—and indeed all animals—come from. Their bodily material goes back to the elements. Those elements have no life, knowledge, power, or other perfection of their own. Such qualities arrive in them as gifts held for a time, and one day those gifts must be returned. While looking at a living body in all its splendour, remember the same materials when they are lifeless and disfigured. That contrast shows where its passing bodily life begins.

The many things are really concepts drawn from the levels of its existence. The soul has a reflected, dependent unity; God's unity is real and not numerical.   296. Imagined forms can serve as mirrors through which we look at something else. It is like an immaterial sun: a universal intellectual reality that contains all its limited, passing instances. The universal concept of the sun is a light that lets the intellect know all the individual suns. While the soul is busy with individual things and its body and powers draw its attention to desirable objects, the universal concept may seem weak. But its weakness is not part of its own nature.   311. A complete world contains everything necessary to its existence and its consequences. The next life is not alongside this world in the same time sequence; its mode is timeless. Those who ask when the Hour will come do not understand the answer “Its knowledge is with my Lord,” because they have not entered the divine presence. The final ends of the worlds are within this world in depth, as stations of truth before the Sovereign, especially in the presence of God and the realm of His names and attributes.   313. The motion and change that produce the soul are those in which each later stage gathers the perfections of the earlier one and adds something more.   314. “Like a heavenly body” refers to its delicacy, clarity, luminosity, and balanced mixture. When opposites are balanced, each is present in a way that resembles its absence.   315. The soul is what makes a person an individual. If old Zayd is the same as young Zayd because the soul preserves their identity, he is also the same person as the fetus. The resurrected person is therefore the very one who obeyed or disobeyed.

  317. If the soul alone individuates a person, as that account says, but resurrection restores the first individual while transmigration makes another, the account seems to require an additional feature—such as the new and old forms matching—to explain identity.

  318. The same soul also remains through transmigration, so on this account it would preserve individuality there as well.

  320. This is the view of those who believe in transmigration: after a soul leaves its body, it enters, for example, an embryo in an animal's womb.

  321. Here, “this” refers to the alleged impossibility of transmigration.

  322. The idea that a heavenly body becomes the setting for a soul's imagination does not mean the soul becomes its soul. The commentator says that Ghazali's reading of Avicenna suggests uncertainty about transmigration because he thinks the heavenly body becomes the soul's own body.

  323. If a soul were inside the body as an accident is inside its subject, it would not be independent enough to have a relation to two possible bodies. A soul free of matter can have such relations without being contained in either body.

  324. The source wording is difficult. The commentator proposes a corrected reading: if the suited, returning soul has received what it is due, then no new soul should flow from the Giver of Forms. “What it is due” is the object of “receives”; “from among the souls” means some of them; the source of the receiving is the soul itself.   325. That is, a heavenly body reveals or gives form to familiar images and desires of the soul.

  326. Transmigration does not mean that a soul leaving a body at death moves into another already living body, since then two souls would inhabit one body. It means that a soul moves into matter ready for it, such as an animal embryo in a womb. How could Avicenna allow a human soul to move into a living heavenly body, which already has both an individual soul and a universal intellective soul? Some philosophers did teach a different system: after long ages, the souls of the heavens complete their development and join the intellects; perfected earthly souls rise to take their place, and another group rises later. That system is a form of transmigration.

  327. The claim that a specific readiness fits each soul does not solve the problem. Dust and ash are not ready for a rational human soul. Nature must first bring matter through the perfections of lower kinds before it can rise to a higher kind. Each form requires suitable matter, readiness, and whatever brings about that readiness. Semen cannot receive the form of an embryo until it first takes on the form of a clinging substance; likewise, the matter of an embryo must first pass through its earlier stages. Though matter is what receives each form, the conditions that make it ready are not simply matter itself. Scattered earthly parts could not receive a soul separated from the body without first becoming ready through the forms closer to that soul.

    ↩

  328. The commentator notes the author's use of a phrase that seems to refer to all pleasures. It is a rhetorical claim, not a sound proof. Removing pain is a kind of absence, and absence cannot itself produce pleasure. The confusion comes from treating something that accompanies pleasure as if it were pleasure itself. Looking at a beautiful face without first being separated from it, hearing a lovely voice, smelling a fragrance, tasting sweetness, or touching a soft body can all be positive pleasures, not relief from pain. God takes joy in His own being, even though religious language about God is carefully defined; He has neither absence nor pain. The same is true of immaterial intellects joined to God.

    ↩

  329. Both replies are weak. The first does not answer why reward or pain should be given if God is not affected by them. The second assumes the conclusion: if the objection stands, there is no reason for a promise or warning whose truth needs to be shown.

    ↩

  330. The afterlife soul is self-sufficient and draws everything it chooses from its own inner reality. The one who gives joy and the one who receives it, or the one who causes fear and the one who feels it, are within the same soul; nothing comes from outside to change it. The commentator compares this with the philosophers' account of God's knowledge: it does not affect God, because it does not come from something outside Him. Our knowledge, by contrast, receives forms from outside, through the Active Intellect and the preparation of our awareness.

    ↩

  331. Worldly things that people grow attached to pass away; those who have not grown close to what lasts will not find it familiar. One might object that their memories of familiar things remain, so they can still enjoy them. The reply gives two reasons they cannot: the horror of the afterlife overwhelms them, and worldly pleasures themselves turn into harm. Wrongfully consuming an orphan's wealth becomes like consuming fire; forbidden food becomes like bitter, poisonous plants. As in the scriptural dream where years of famine and plenty appear as lean and fat cows, a person who devoured orphans' wealth unjustly will perceive themselves as eating fire.

    ↩

  332. The ordinary, untrained person relies mainly on sense, imagination, and instinct. Without the strength of an example, they would not be reassured. Even if reason were present, without examples suited to it, it would argue with reason and resist understanding abstract realities.

    ↩

  333. The person in question believed what the Prophet brought, did their best, and sincerely committed to an interpretation. Ghazali also says that the things promised in revelation can exist in five ways: in themselves, intellectually, in imagination, through the senses, or by likeness. Anyone who accepts one of these ways is not to be declared an unbeliever. Only someone who denies all meaning and rejects the promise entirely is an unbeliever.

  334. This includes rules for trade, marriage, inheritance, and related matters.

    ↩

  335. The commentator says that the verse's phrase “at an appointed time” answers the objection: it names a timeless, eternal day, not a day within ordinary time.   336. “Returns to God and is gathered to Him” means that the person is annihilated in God and lives through Him: outwardly they have their form in this world, but their inner meaning is with God, where the Hour is known. In their bodily aspect they remain here; in spirit they are in the world beyond nature or in the divine realm. Likewise, their natural body is in time while their spirit is in a higher timeless duration, and their inner meaning is in eternity. Whatever appears there is the form of what exists here; knowledge is the seed of direct vision. The note quotes Persian verses meaning: “Many ask about the Day of Judgment as if they were already there,” and “Whoever has not seen the Beloved's face directly today is like a child waiting for tomorrow.”

  337. “On the face of the earth” can mean the body's ground or the ground of material readiness. It may also mean that as long as someone remains here, there is still a knower and something known, and the Hour has not yet come for them.

  338. This phrase echoes the Qur'anic “in a seat of truth, with a Sovereign who is all-powerful.” The divine presence is a fitting replacement for standing by the body and clinging to the earth.

  339. The commentator lists five meanings of “grave.” First, the body is the grave of the soul, as in the Persian saying, “The souls of the dead are in the grave of the body.” Second, it is the familiar physical grave where the body is buried. Third, it is the imaginal body described in the main text. Fourth, for the soul, it is the set of conditions surrounding it: worldly distractions press in on the soul, sins and ignorance darken it, and knowledge is light. Fifth, for souls free of matter, it is the world of pure intellect. The graves and shrines of these souls are the places the nearest angels visit and surround.

  340. The author answers an objection to spiritual resurrection: if the powers that perceive individual things depend on matter, they perish with the body, while the intellect that survives cannot perceive particulars. He replies that these powers exist in an imaginal, nonmaterial way. They remain with the soul and continue to imagine, understand, and sense particular things.

    ↩

  341. These forms are shadows of the soul's bright or dark qualities from this life: its good works and knowledge, or the worldly distractions and narrow limits that weighed it down.

    ↩

  342. The forms of the next life are the same as the imaginal forms of the intermediate state in their basic nature. They differ in strength, weakness, completeness, and attention. In the intermediate state, a person is still turned toward this world; in the next life, this world is forgotten and attention turns fully toward the forms of the afterlife. The intermediate state is like a dream, and this life is like a dream within a dream.

    ↩

  343. Desire appears as a pig, anger as a wild beast, and deceit as a demon. A person ruled by these natural urges is like someone who serves them and carries out their orders. God says, “Do not worship Satan,” and asks, “Have you seen the one who takes their own desire as their god?”

    ↩

  344. The reference is to the first level of the power of imagination, which leads back to what philosophers call the material intellect. The account must explain both what remains after death and what is still only a capacity. The author identifies it with imagination because this is the final form reached by the natural powers in this life and the first basis for the forms of the next.

  345. Even if matter and form were only joined together rather than united as one thing, they would still need a shared nature and a close fit. This point does not depend on their being one.

  346. Here, smells and sounds are examples of forms that air receives; the pronouns in the Arabic refer to air.   347. Here, “matter” means any underlying basis for something, not only the material that carries an added quality.

    ↩

  348. The author says that those who notice this will see that imagined and understood forms are more noble, complete, and powerful because their basis is finer. Many people think they are weaker and less important, especially when they treat mental images as mere copies of physical things.   349. “Inner causes” here means a person's habits and character traits.

  350. The first verse looks at each person's own place and the preserved core within them. The verses about God's rule look instead at the dropping away of relationships and ranks.   351. The commentator has already listed several meanings of “grave.” One is the set of habits and deeds, bright or dark, that surround the soul after death. The “grave” and “place of sleep” in the question, “Who woke us from our place of sleep?” are the shadows and forms that enclose the soul between death and Resurrection. These forms grow stronger and more complete as the soul turns away from this world and toward the next, whether in kindness or severity. Resurrection is this waking and full development. The intermediate state is like sleep; resurrection is waking from weak forms and taking on stronger ones.

  352. In reason and in the word's ordinary sense, we are already gathered to God: our existence is hidden and erased beneath His. In the religious sense, this gathering is still to come. It occurs when we leave behind our natural bodies, take on pure forms of the intermediate world, and are gathered through them toward God's expressions of kindness or severity. It is the return of meaning and form to their source.

  353. The commentator explains the seventy-cubit chain through the ties that hold a person back from God. He says that human existence has seven subtle levels, each with ten parts. These are the ten portions from which Adam’s nature was formed: one from the elements and nine from the nine heavenly spheres. Love, for example, is linked to Venus and anger to Mars. The elemental portion at each level refers to earthly qualities and the ability to be affected. In counting the seventy ties, he says to count the final effects and leave out their starting points.

    If each of the seventy ties is seen as reflecting a thousand of God’s beautiful names, they make seventy thousand veils of light and darkness, as in a well-known report. Their existence is light, while their limited nature is darkness. For the unhappy, the seventy ties remain only potential and never become a path to God. Even when they become active in a person’s nature and soul, they are like fire if they do not lead to God. Since the person does not see or reflect God’s names, these ties have no living connection with Him; together they form the chain seventy cubits long.

    The commentator then gives another way to count these ties. He divides people into seven groups linked to the seven planets: rulers and commanders to the Sun; soldiers to Mars; clerks and accountants to Mercury; scholars and advisers to Jupiter; farmers and people who live in caves or mountains to Saturn; musicians, lovers of adornment, women, and noblewomen to Venus; and travelers and merchants to the Moon. Each group depends on things that support bodily life, such as money. The commentator lists ten kinds of attachment, based on the astrologer’s houses: money; siblings and relatives; property, parents, servants, and animals; children; spouses and partners; young people; misfortunes; people with authority over us; friends; and enemies and large animals. He leaves out the first house because it stands for the self, not an attachment, and the ninth because it stands for knowledge and virtues, which perfect the soul rather than tie it down. Seven groups multiplied by ten attachments make seventy ties that keep the soul from reaching God.

    The seventy thousand veils arise because each tie contains a thousand particular concerns. The commentator compares them with the many tasks Adam needed after coming down to earth to obtain even a bite of food, according to a report. Bright veils include family and knowledge when they are not directed toward God; dark veils include money, property, animals, and similar worldly things.

    ↩

  355. The “wild beasts” include the animal traits that follow from a person's habits. They may also include real animals, though those are gathered only as a secondary part of the event.

  358. If a person's habits are good, their forms are smooth-faced and youthful; if their habits are bad, their forms are dark and blue.

Those who turn toward God are like people absorbed in the sea itself. Its greatness keeps them from being distracted by waves and bubbles, except as signs of its works and appearances. The sea is the lasting reality beneath them. The mystic says: “When the court of Truth appears, the traveler who trusted in illusion will be ashamed.”

  375. The two reports do not conflict. “Every child is born with a sound nature” refers to the spirit, which comes from a pure, protected world. “The fortunate person is fortunate in the womb, and the unhappy person is unhappy in the womb” refers to the body's nature and temperament, which may be sound or unsound.   376. This natural worship means following the commands and limits built into creation, just as religious worship means following God's revealed commands and limits. Both aim to bring a person closer to God. Religious worship also keeps people away from Hell; natural worship draws them away from matter and the lowest levels of nature. Whoever is shaped by spiritual qualities is more open to God's mercy; whoever is ruled by bodily nature moves farther from it. This is why the world is called cursed, along with those who are wholly caught up in it—not those whose bodies are here while their hearts have risen above it. The complete person's simple intellect belongs to the highest, lasting realm, not to time or place, even though their body remains in both. The awake mind knows that references to dates, places, and positions describe only the body's life; the simple intellect is free of them.

  377. The body, as a whole shaped and made one by the soul, does not simply perish. The soul gives it its identity, individuality, and unity. The scattered elements of the body, considered apart from the soul, are not the body itself; they remain much as they were before and after death.

  382. The goal is for the soul to be gathered in a complete state, not an incomplete one. This requires it to be given enough time to grow.

  388. This refers to the question, “For what purpose is it?” The purpose meant here is the final end.

  389. In The Divine Things, the author raises a problem about the principle that the nobler being must come before the lower. They are all faces of God and His light, joined to Him in a real, inner connection. There is no actual infinity of separate beings here, only infinitely many ranks within one connected reality.

  392. The intellect is not merely like an image in a mirror. It is the image itself, and the mirror is only a comparison. As we have seen, it has no separate essence of its own, so there is no actual mirror here.

  393. The author proves unity in two ways: first, by showing that what is understood in itself is united with the intellect that understands it; second, by showing that knowledge is united with the one who knows.

The author assumes that these intellects exist necessarily through God, since their necessity and lasting life come from Him.

  396. A soul reaches a state of purity by gaining the right qualities in this life. The next life is not a place to earn those qualities; it is where what a person has done comes into view. The note's phrase “because of the strength of longing” means that the soul longs strongly to be drawn toward it.

  397. Every animal has a form and a meaning: a body and a soul. Each develops through inner change during its life in this world. God gives each being a set time to develop. It then joins the other souls of its kind while each remains distinct. The intellect that rules the kind is a broad unity, not a small, countable group; its light is wide enough to hold all their souls and imaginal forms.

  399. This refers to those who say that the soul first arises from the body, then continues after death through inner change, or even before that change. These include some Aristotelians and many religious thinkers who say that the soul is free of matter in its essence but begins with the body.

  400. This is a comparison between the greater world and the smaller world of the human body.

  401. The spirits were not present as separate beings in the unfolding world. They existed together in God's eternal knowledge, distinct there because God's knowledge includes every detail. The general state means this undivided existence; the detailed state means the many meanings and forms of things, which some call the “fixed essences.”

  402. This applies to written letters if we mean the letters that a natural pen is ready to write. But it does not explain the letters that exist in the universe.   404. Simple forms are like separate letters; the spirits of compound bodies are like letters joined into words.

  405. A Persian poet says: “I always live in the writer's hand; He keeps me between two fingers. My own being has no movement in it; He moves me at every moment.” The two fingers mean the qualities of beauty and majesty, or gentleness and force.

  408. The “book of the soul” means the soul's inner record, written through its habits and qualities.

  410. The soul comes before the body in its own nature and in a timeless sense. It gives the body its individual identity. We have already shown that a body cannot choose one special form over another for no reason. The body is not first an empty, identical thing that later receives any form. The mistake comes from confusing what exists outside the mind with what we understand in thought.

    ↩

  411. Ibn Arabi does not deny that the body follows the soul, whether we mean the usual human body or the slow-witted person in the form they take in the intermediate world.

  412. “The same body” means the body whose form makes it the body it is, and whose individual identity comes from its soul and existence. The commentator also wants to protect religious teaching and the beliefs of ordinary Muslims. As the author has said, the well-known teaching is that on the Day of Resurrection this is the same body and the same soul. The difference lies in the qualities of each state: worldly, intermediate, or next-life.

    ↩

  413. The plant has something like touch-awareness. If it truly had the sense of touch, it would be an animal, since touch distinguishes animals. It would also move by its own choice. But nature rises from lower to higher in order, so the plant cannot have full touch-awareness.

  414. God gives the plant a set time to develop its form and soul. The author wrote earlier about particular animal souls in a way that also applies here.

  415. These trees are not separate from the heavenly trees; they are contained within them. They also include trees formed from human habits and actions. In paradise, the ground is ready for planting, and its plants are words of praise to God.

  416. The Lote Tree is described in Qur'anic commentary as standing to the right of the Throne, above the seventh heaven. The knowledge of every angel ends there, and what rises to heaven or descends from above passes through it. The tree is covered by what covers it. The commentator reads it as the Great Intermediate World, the end of the journey of perfected souls and their actions and knowledge, and the highest level of God's names. Angels gathering around it like ravens means that those who travel toward God reach their end there. There is no village beyond Abadan. On this reading, the Lote Tree means a blessed state of wonder, as in the Prophet's prayer, “Lord, increase me in wonder of You,” and Ibn al-Farid's line: “I think the limit of waking and drunkenness is my ascent toward her; my home lies at the farthest point of the Lote Tree.” The word for the tree is also linked to an illness of the head called sudar.

  417. I repeat this point because the evidence that existence is the same as these qualities, and that their levels follow the levels of existence, can be seen by looking at the human soul. This is even clearer when we look at intellect and what lies above it. The soul is knowledge, will, and love through its very being. Its being is at once awareness of itself and its powers, present knowledge of itself, life, light, and the ability to act through all its powers. The same is true, even more fully, of intellect and what lies above it. In extended bodies, however, completeness in every quality is also a lack in every quality.

  418. The author does not mean that the forms that flow into matter are themselves gathered after death, since they belong to this worldly life. He means that they are gathered in the same way as simple beings are.

  420. These are imaginal forms, also called suspended images.

  421. The phrase means that the Illuminationists say these forms exist; it does not mean they say the forms are directly connected to the separate intellects.   422. They are called “soul-forms” because they are images in the separate imagination of the Universal Soul, much as images in a person's imagination are soul-forms for that person.   423. The “matter of intellect” here means imaginal forms, in line with the author's own account. The “matter of soul” means sensible forms. Each is called matter because it is joined to its form, changes into it, and becomes it.

    ↩

  424. This refers to the wonders that the images of the intellectual world contain.

    ↩

  425. This means that each being longs for a real inner union with its source, and for direct knowledge of it. The passage also concerns the intellects of rising human souls, as the author's next words show.

    ↩

  426. These forms are not dark and made of matter. They exist more completely and clearly than physical forms. Nor are they merely imaginary; they can be seen. To be seen means to take a form that the shared sense can perceive, whether that form comes from inside or outside. The outward senses are only pathways that lead to this shared power of perception, like five rivers flowing into one pool.

  427. The proof that the visible world reveals these hidden forms is that natural processes ripen bodies and plants and change them. Nature itself is like a fire with three flames. Imagine what happens when it changes and appears in another world, with its chains, shackles, scorpions, and snakes.

  428. Matter, decay, and passing away belong only to this world. If their features were carried into another world, there would not be more than one kind of world. In brief, fully formed beings return to intellect; extended things that hold together or flow away return to the pit of matter; and matter returns to destruction, because lack rules over it. As we said earlier, powers and unrealized possibilities return to matter, while complete forms return to the source of complete forms. This does not contradict the truth that all things return to God, because even the weakest existence returns to Him, and judgments follow what is strongest in each thing.

  429. Just as matter and the pit of nonexistence are the end of physical things considered only as bodies, and of people who reject nature's commands, Hell is the end of souls that reject God's moral and religious commands.

  430. In contrast, wise and intellectual ends belong to the long upward path. Their starting points are mistaken ideas suited only to false arguments, empty hopes, and desires opposed to true rational aims. Here, “tyrant” means a specific power of desire or a particular craving. These goals move further into nonexistence as they become more limited and fade away, as we see when trivial aims of the past vanish. A wise person says, “How sorry I am for what I neglected in my duty to God.”

  431. What happens to all happens to each one. As God says, “Your creation and your rising are only like the creation and rising of one soul.” After natural forms are complete, the first blowing brings them death and decay. A second blowing brings fear and collapse to the souls that have completed their development; it puts out their light. In the next blowing, their fire and greater light are kindled: the souls receive imaginal forms through God's breath. So one form dies and another lives. The author will explain this later.

  432. This is the imaginal earth, lit by its Lord's light—the divine light that guides the soul. It is like many pieces of wood and wicks lit by a great fire. When the author says that this may mean the earth we know, he means any earth, simple or compound, including bodies. He says “after it has been taken into God's hand” because the verse appears in the context of Resurrection, after the blowing that brings death and before the books of deeds are placed and the prophets and witnesses are brought forward. The earth can also mean the fullest capacity to receive existence, and God's complete light and unity.

    ↩

  433. This interpretation leads to another, and the verses are connected in the chapter of The Groups. But the verse about God's hand comes before the others, so the commentator turns to explain it here.

  434. We have already seen that only a weak trace like matter remains at the edge of the heavenly body's form. Its resistance to outside change comes from its soul, not its body. This supports the idea that the heavens are folded up.

    ↩

  435. The fire and other forms exist hidden within matter and then appear from it. Matter contains all forms only as possibilities; a form is what makes a thing actual, while matter is only what makes it possible.

    ↩

  436. This is the imaginal form that corresponds to the natural form.

    ↩

  437. This supports the author's claim that these forms have life in their own right.

    ↩

  438. In all five places, “this fire” means the soul-form. “The fire in the higher world” means the first, intellectual fire.

  439. Up to the phrase “plants of the earth,” the philosopher gives examples that are not true as they sound and cannot be used as proof. If he means the compound earth, then it includes plant life and minerals, which may have an active inner form. But his goal is to prove an active form within the simple earth, even though earth should receive action rather than act. So words like “growth” and “sprouting” should mean the earth's cooling, drying, and holding forms together. The earth's inner soul-form guides these actions.

  440. I must say that Ibn Arabi's insight is very deep, and deserves to be written in gold, not ink. “Life” can mean the source of perception and action, as when we say a living thing is aware and active. This is the life usually attributed to spirits. It belongs to spirits naturally, but to bodies only through something else. “Life” can also mean simple, all-pervading existence. We have often called this “the life that flows through everything.” In that sense, it belongs to all things that exist, including bodies. How could it not, when a body exists, and existence is life in each thing according to its level?

    When great philosophers call bodies decaying, dead, or dark, they mean the first kind of life. It comes to bodies from spirits, so they have one life of their own and another received from outside. It is strange that the author says this here, when he repeatedly teaches in this book and elsewhere that life, knowledge, and will follow from existence or are the same as it. I have often shown this rule by looking at the rational soul: its existence is its knowledge of itself, its life, light, will, and love of itself. It is also its power to take on many states through its powers and images. For the author and other knowers, the soul is existence itself.

    When Ibn Arabi says that stones and crafted vessels have forms of life, he means existence, though it is a passing existence received from another. His statement that bodies remember and praise God is also true. The author establishes this in his early discussion of general principles, and I have explained it in my notes. When we set aside the differences between things, their praise is included in God's own praise, as the verse says, “There is nothing that does not praise Him.” That is, each thing praises God through its own existence.

    ↩

  441. If “speech” means human speech, then animals do not have it either. But if it means each thing's own kind of speech, then everything speaks and is guided to what it was made for. Every existence is a word. Seen as coming from God, it is God's word; seen as belonging to its own nature, it is that nature's word. It describes God's qualities and displays His names. Praise describes the praised one's qualities and gifts, and the existence that flows through all things praises itself in this way.

    ↩

  442. Ibn Arabi's wording keeps the different levels in view, even if one level is only a shadow of a light or a branch of a source.

    ↩

  443. The verses about all things praising God show that existence, wherever it is, has life, knowledge, awareness, and will. Ibn Arabi himself says that God is with us wherever we are.

    ↩

  444. The author could say that bodies are dead and dark compared with the animal life that enables awareness and action. But they are not dead compared with the deeper life that belongs to existence and flows through all things. “We made every living thing from water” means that life arises from the life of existence. Even matter, which is lower than bodies, is alive in this sense because it exists. The author's statement that bodies are mixed with absence already shows that they have existence.

    If relative death and darkness made them unable to be alive, aware, or praising in any sense, then they would also be dead in relation to the highest life: knowledge of God, His qualities, and His actions. People who know God would then be alive, while others were dead. How could the praise of all things show that all things have life? We do not deny the life and praise of imaginal bodies or other forms. But life has three levels: general, special, and most special, as we have explained.

    ↩

  445. This interpretation changes Ibn Arabi's meaning. He clearly says that life belongs to bodies in their own right, not that they receive it from outside.

  446. The root meaning of “the Hour” may be “striving” or “moving quickly,” as some dictionaries suggest. One may explain the word by saying that “the Hour” comes from this root. The Qur'an uses it for the brief moment when the Resurrection begins, a short time in which a great event takes place. The author says the word also points to the fact that Resurrection is hidden within the world of nature and is part of the soul's long upward journey. This is why people see it at different distances: God says they think it is far away, while He sees it as near. It may be called a “day,” as in the verse that describes a day lasting fifty thousand years; it may be called an “hour”; or it may be even shorter, “like the blink of an eye, or shorter still.” The return to God is like the beginning of creation.

    ↩

  447. What happens to all happens to each one. As the verse says, “Your creation and your rising are only like the creation and rising of one soul.” Each soul reaches its end and becomes independent of the body and its powers. In the same way, all things move toward their ends and return to their source, until they reach the final end. The smaller hours are included in the Great Hour, but sense and imagination cannot grasp the whole of this movement. Even the intellect can know it only in a general way: everything moves toward its end through an endless chain of inner change. The time of one limited change is limited, but the time of endlessly many changes has no end. Compared with the Source of all sources, however, it is like the blink of an eye, or even shorter.

    ↩

  448. Light and forms may be imagined as a cone, with its point at the world beyond matter and its broad base at the material world—or the other way around. If we focus on simplicity and unity, the point belongs to the world beyond matter, where things are most simple and united, while the material world is divided and mixed. If we focus on the amount of existence, the world beyond matter is wider, and the material world is the narrow point.

The author then explains that the first ends natural forms and the second strengthens the link between spirits and simple imaginal forms. The first form dies; the second is used and brought to life.

  451. A report says that a sound is made in the horn as many times as there are creatures. This points to the meaning just described.

  452. “The eye” here means either the form itself and its inner reality, or the sight of that imaginal form. It can be called the “eye” because the senses in that world are joined; each sense does the work of all the others.

  453. Rather, they are people of God. They are not subject to changing worlds or time, because they are not the spheres and bodies made of elements that come into being and pass away. In their inner reality, they are simple intellects and spirits sent free of place, time, and direction. Their home is the world of divine power; their time is the highest, rightward realm; their direction is a spiritual ascent through light. They rise like the angels who are near to God. A Persian poem says: “When I became empty of myself, I knew nothing but God. I disappeared from myself and remained through the Real; my garment of being was torn open at once.”

  454. The great Resurrection belongs to an upward path through levels of being, not to a point on the ordinary timeline. That is why the Prophet was taught to answer questions about its timing by saying, “Its knowledge is with my Lord.” Anyone who tries to find its time by looking ahead along ordinary time is making the same mistake as someone who looks backward in time to find the eternal Source. It is like mistaking a swelling for something substantial. Thinkers find this difficult, let alone people who rely mainly on imagination. The author says that the Day of the great Resurrection is to the small resurrections of each breath as a day is to its hours, or a year to its days. Mawlana says, in effect: “Who would ask when the great Gathering will come, while it is already gathering all things?”

    ↩

  455. The signs of the great Resurrection have counterparts in the small one. When the earth shakes on that day, the body's ground shakes at death and its structure trembles. When the earth and mountains are lifted and crushed, the body's bones are crushed. When the stars are darkened, the lights of the body's powers go out. When the sun is folded up and the moon darkens, the spirit of the heart—the sun of the small world—comes to an end, and the light of the spirit in the brain, which depends on the heart, fades. When all creatures are gathered to God, the soul's many powers are gathered into one simple spiritual self.

    ↩

  456. This refers to God's fullest revelation of Himself through His names “the One,” “the Unique,” and “the All-Subduing.” Individual natures disappear, and all existence returns to God; the link between existence and separate natures falls away. Before the great Resurrection, beings appear as many and are linked to their individual natures. At the Resurrection, even separate intellects lose that distinction, because every trace of otherness is overcome. In this account, the natural world is the world of what is separate from God.

  457. They exist in a fuller and brighter way, as explained earlier.

  458. This upward return is a rise in the order of being, not movement through space. The soul rises as it is uncovered and freed from its coverings. The Resurrection of ordinary people, whose goals and rewards still take bodily form, is not the same as the Resurrection of those who have reached the truth and attained the highest qualities they could receive from God. The author alludes to the end of Avicenna's The Healing, where the fully realized person is described as a human being shaped by divine qualities.

  464. This refers to people whose intermediate world remains inactive. May God protect us from that.

  471. These are people of high resolve who cut off their ties to the world all at once. A Persian verse says: “Take one step beyond yourself; the next lies in the Friend's lane.”

  477. These are people who sin openly, unlike those who keep their faults hidden.

  478. People may fast to obey God, to clear the heart—for hunger is a cloud that rains wisdom—to understand the poor, or to take on the quality of the Self-Sufficient, who does not eat.   482. A traditional prayer addressed to the Imams calls them “the greatest path and the most upright way.”

  485. Knowledge is included among deeds, since it is an act of the heart. The record contains three kinds of forms: states and settled traits, which are both effects and sources of deeds; corresponding images that appear in the soul; and conscious representations of the deeds. Even now, despite all the veils and distractions, a person can look back and see their deeds imprinted in the book of the self. How much clearer will they be when the veil is lifted?

  486. The agents that record different kinds of things include the Active Intellect for universal forms, souls embedded in matter, suspended images, divine forms, and subtle ties corresponding to individual things.

  487. A good deed leads to another good deed until goodness becomes a settled trait.

  488. Good traits form ranks of angels—beautiful youths and everlasting boys, or good influences and choices in this life. Every thought and action points toward more good.   489. Saying that the angel and devil have “one substance” points to the unity of what is named. Scripture also speaks of punishing angels. The angelic trait has a side that displays God's overpowering power.

  490. These forms are like souls embedded in matter and like universal souls and intellects. They exist in a partial form at the lower level, and in a universal form at the higher level. The lower forms are held within the higher ones.
